captions: Part eight. In April twenty twenty six, Mem0
replaced this algorithm. Let's see what changed, and
why.
The old pipeline spent two LLM calls per
turn: one to extract, one to diff against
existing memory.
The new one makes a single call, and
it only ever adds.
Mem0's reasoning: the model spends its capacity on
understanding the input, rather than diffing against existing
state.
Nothing is overwritten. When a fact changes, the
new one lives alongside the old one.
And the external graph database is gone from
the open source version, replaced by lightweight, built-in
entity linking.
Why drop the graph from the open source
version? Mem0 hasn't published a full rationale, but
the evidence points one way.
Cost: a graph means extra LLM calls and
a graph database on every write.
Mixed results: in the paper, it helped temporal
questions, but not multi-hop ones.
Entity links keep the most useful part, an
index from who and what, to memories, at
a fraction of the cost.
And graph memory is still available on Mem0's
hosted platform.
Here's the new write path, straight from the
code.
Gather context: the last ten messages from this
session.
Retrieve the top ten related memories, and map
their ids to small integers.
Then one LLM call extracts every new fact,
from both the user and the assistant, and
links each one to related memories.
Relative dates, like last week, are resolved against
the conversation's date, so they stay meaningful forever.
The new facts are embedded in one batch,
and exact duplicates are dropped with an MD5
hash.
They're stored, and logged to history as ADD
events. And finally, entity linking runs.
One prompt detail deserves its own moment.
A memory that says, went to Paris last
week, is useless six months later.
So the extraction prompt receives an observation date,
the day the conversation happened, and must rewrite
every relative time against it. Yesterday, last week,
next month.
Went to Paris last week becomes, went to
Paris the week of the fifteenth of May.
It's told explicitly not to use today's date
for this, because memories can be ingested long
after the conversation took place.
Entity linking replaces the graph.
spaCy pulls entities out of each new memory:
proper nouns, quoted titles, and multi-word noun phrases
like machine learning.
Each entity is normalized and embedded, then matched
against a separate entity collection, by exact text,
or by a cosine similarity of at least
zero point nine five.
A match gets this memory's id appended to
its linked memories. Otherwise, a new entity is
created.
The result is a lightweight index, from things,
to the memories that mention them.
Now the read path.
The query is lemmatized with spaCy, so attending
and attend match.
It's embedded, and semantic search over-fetches: four times
the requested results, and at least sixty candidates.
In parallel, BM25 keyword search scores the same
store.
Entity matching adds a boost to memories linked
to the query's entities.
Then the three signals are fused into one
score.
BM25 deserves a closer look.
For each query term, it multiplies how rare
the term is across all memories by how
often it appears in this one. Repeats saturate,
so saying bengaluru five times doesn't win, and
long memories are normalized against the average length.
The raw score has no upper bound, so
Mem0 squashes it with a logistic sigmoid.
Longer queries naturally produce bigger raw scores, so
the sigmoid's midpoint moves up with query length.
For a four to six term query, a
raw score of three becomes point zero eight.
Seven becomes exactly one half. Nine becomes point
seven seven, and twelve, point nine five.
Here's the fusion formula, exactly as it appears
in the code.
Take a query: which city did Riya move
to, for work?
First, a gate. Any candidate whose semantic score
is below the threshold, zero point one by
default, is dropped, whatever its keywords say.
Raw BM25 scores are unbounded, so they're squashed
with a sigmoid. Its midpoint and steepness depend
on query length. For four to six terms:
midpoint seven, steepness zero point six.
The entity boost is the entity similarity, times
zero point five, times a small penalty for
entities linked to very many memories.
Add the three, divide by the maximum possible,
two and a half with every signal active,
and sort.
Watch how keyword and entity signals lift the
right memory to the top. And notice: BM25
can reorder candidates, but it never adds new
ones.
One more detail in that entity boost.
The boost is multiplied by one, over one
plus a thousandth of n minus one, squared,
where n is how many memories the entity
links to.
An entity linked to one memory keeps its
full weight. Ten memories: still point nine two
five. Thirty: point five four. Sixty: point two
two. A hundred: under point one.
Why? An entity that appears everywhere, like the
user's own name, says almost nothing about which
memory is relevant. It's the same idea as
inverse document frequency in BM25.
Mem0 reports big gains.
On LoCoMo, the open-source score rose from seventy
one point four to ninety one point six.
The platform blog reports ninety two and a
half.
On LongMemEval, ninety four point four.
And on BEAM, a newer benchmark at one
million and ten million tokens, sixty four point
one, and forty eight point six, showing how
hard truly huge histories remain.
All at roughly seven thousand tokens per query,
versus twenty five thousand plus for full context.
Two caveats. These are vendor-reported numbers, and they
use a different setup from the paper, so
don't compare them directly to its sixty six
point nine.
Add-only isn't free.
If Riya lived in Pune and now lives
in Bengaluru, both facts are in the store.
Retrieval, and the answering model, must work out
which one is current, using timestamps and linked
memories.
Mem0 itself lists temporal reasoning and multi-session reasoning
as open problems.
The design moved complexity from write time to
read time. That's a deliberate bet: writes stay
cheap and lossless, and reads get smarter.
